name: Cardio / zone 2 for leanness

lead: Zone 2 cardio is steady, conversational-pace aerobic exercise, commonly placed at roughly 60 to 70 percent of maximum heart rate. People use it to burn calories and lower body fat, aiming for a leaner face and body without hard training that cuts into lifting recovery.

At this intensity fat is the main fuel, and sources report that aerobic exercise promotes weight loss, with fat loss being a whole-body result of energy balance rather than targeted to one area. Public-health bodies recommend about 2.5 hours of moderate aerobic exercise a week for health. High-intensity intervals can deliver similar benefits in less time, and zone 2 has no universally accepted definition.

paras: People walk briskly on an incline, cycle, row or use an elliptical for 30 to 60 minutes several times a week, often on non-lifting days or after training. It is combined with a calorie deficit and strength work. Body-fat changes build over weeks to months.

Reported risks include overuse injury, overtraining, and low-energy-availability problems in high-volume athletes who under-fuel. People with heart conditions or who are new to exercise are commonly advised to build up gradually.

angle.text: Users do steady low-intensity cardio to burn calories and lower body fat, which brings a leaner face and body into view. Aerobic exercise is well studied for health and weight, and zone 2 specifically for leanness is still debated.

lead: Cardio for leanness is the use of aerobic exercise, including low-intensity steady-state work often called zone 2, to lower body fat and look leaner. A lower body-fat percentage shows up as sharper abdominal and muscle definition, a more defined jawline and cheekbones, and a slimmer overall frame, which is why leanmaxxing guides routinely pair it with diet and lifting.[1][2][3]

Zone 2 has no universally accepted definition, but in the common five-zone heart-rate model it sits at roughly 60 to 70 percent of maximum heart rate, where fat is the main fuel and slow-twitch muscle fibres do most of the work.[1] Proponents describe it as a sustainable way to add weekly energy expenditure and to build aerobic fitness at the same time; walking, cycling, rowing, incline treadmill work and Peloton rides are the formats that come up most often in training logs.[2][4]

Zone 2 moved from endurance-coaching jargon into mainstream fitness talk largely through longevity media, notably physician Peter Attia's podcast and his 2023 book Outlive, which sold close to three million copies by October 2025 according to CBS reporting summarised on Wikipedia.[5] In looksmaxxing spaces the same idea is folded into leanmaxxing, the pursuit of a low body-fat look.[6][7]

Encyclopedic sources note that regular aerobic exercise promotes weight loss and that public-health bodies recommend about 2.5 hours of moderate activity a week, while high-intensity interval training is described as delivering similar benefits in less time.[2][8] A 2025 narrative review in Sports Medicine by Storoschuk, Moran-MacDonald, Gibala and Gurd examined the case for zone 2 specifically and concluded that current evidence does not show it to be optimal for mitochondrial or fat-oxidation capacity.[9] Fat loss is understood to be whole-body rather than targeted, so facial leanness is reached through overall fat reduction.[10]

paras: Aerobic exercise is sustained activity such as running, cycling, swimming or walking that relies mainly on aerobic energy production.[2] Zone 2 is the low-intensity band of that work. Depending on the system, it may be defined by heart rate, power, pace or perceived exertion, and it is often described as a pace at which a person can still hold a conversation.[1]

In the five-zone model, zone 2 is about 60 to 70 percent of maximum heart rate. During it, fat is the main fuel, type I (slow-twitch) fibres are mostly recruited, and lactate is cleared about as fast as it is produced.[1] Other models use more or fewer zones, so the label does not always mean the same thing; one T Nation training log, for example, describes a Peloton session in which zone 3 of a seven-zone scale was used for the hard efforts and zone 2 for recovery.[4]

The stated goal of zone 2 work in endurance sport is to raise aerobic performance by increasing mitochondrial density and fat oxidation, so that a given pace or power can be held at a lower heart rate and perceived effort.[1]

Aerobic exercise as a concept has a long history. British physiologist A. V. Hill introduced maximal oxygen uptake in 1922; Kenneth Cooper coined the term aerobics in 1966 and published his book in 1968; and Jane Fonda's 1982 workout video helped make home aerobics popular worldwide.[2]

Zone-based training comes from endurance sport, where coaches divide intensity into bands relative to heart rate, power or lactate. Zone 2 sits in the lower band, below the lactate threshold.[1][9] The term entered general fitness conversation much later, through longevity and health podcasts. Peter Attia, a Canadian-American physician who launched The Peter Attia Drive in 2018 and published Outlive in 2023, treats exercise as a leading longevity tool, and Wikipedia reports that exercise physiologist Inigo San Millan's work on zone 2 became central to his own regimen, including roughly an hour of stationary cycling several times a week.[5]

High-intensity interval training grew alongside it. Izumi Tabata's 1996 study of Olympic speed skaters used 20-second hard efforts with 10 seconds of rest and reported aerobic gains similar to steady-state work in far less time; Martin Gibala's group at McMaster published low-volume protocols in 2010 and 2011, and a 2012 BBC Horizon segment brought the approach to wide audiences.[8]

At low intensity the body relies mostly on fat for fuel, and faster-acting glycogen takes over as intensity rises.[2] Proponents in fitness communities say this makes zone 2 an efficient fat-burning zone. The Wikipedia article on aerobic exercise states that low or moderate intensity is less efficient for fat loss than high intensity, though that passage carries a verification flag, and it attributes fat reduction to lipolysis across the body rather than to fuel burned during the session.[2]

Exercise physiologists distinguish the intensity where fat oxidation peaks (often called FATmax) from the aerobic threshold. A 2024 study of 761 untrained adults aged 41 to 68, using a cycling test with gas analysis, found maximal fat oxidation occurred at lower relative work rates than the aerobic threshold in every fitness group and that the two measures agreed weakly, indicating they mark different physiological points.[9] This is one reason numbers quoted for the best fat-burning intensity differ between sources.

Research on spot reduction, including a 2011 trial of 24 sedentary adults who did abdominal exercises five days a week for six weeks, found no decrease in abdominal subcutaneous fat even as core endurance improved.[10] A comparison of the dominant and non-dominant forearms of high-level tennis players, summarised on Wikipedia, likewise found larger muscle but equal subcutaneous fat.[10] On this basis, facial and abdominal leanness are understood to follow overall fat loss, with genetics influencing where fat is lost first.[10]

The central debate is whether easy steady cardio or hard intervals is the better route to leanness and fitness. Wikipedia reports that a 2017 trial found HIIT comparable to prolonged continuous training for reducing abdominal visceral fat in obese young women, and a 2018 meta-analysis found HIIT time-efficient for reducing abdominal and visceral fat, with modest subcutaneous fat loss in healthy people and larger loss in overweight people. Earlier work in 2010 suggested HIIT might be less effective than longer sessions for obesity.[8]

The 2025 Storoschuk review argues that the media case for zone 2 rests mostly on observational data from elite endurance athletes training at high volumes, that substantial evidence supports high-intensity exercise for mitochondrial capacity and cardiometabolic health, and that training above zone 2 matters most when total volume is low.[9] Zone 2 advocates counter, as described in longevity media, that easy sessions are sustainable, add weekly energy expenditure and leave more recovery for lifting.[5]

Seen from a looksmaxxing angle, the practical difference is recovery cost: hard intervals tax the legs and nervous system, which matters for people who are also trying to build or keep muscle, while low-intensity work is easier to stack onto a training week.[8]

On looksmax.org, cardio is discussed under the heading of leanmaxxing, the pursuit of a low body-fat appearance. One thread titled "Cardio" includes a reply saying cardio is for someone "leanmaxxing", in answer to an original poster who wants to remove face fat.[6] Other threads ask for a "final consensus" on cardio for leanmaxxing, what cardio and diet to use to maintain a lean look, and how to lose fat efficiently with cardio and diet alone.[7][11][12]

Another recurring topic is the interaction with muscle building: a thread asks how detrimental cardio is for staying vascular while growing muscle, reflecting a common concern that endurance work might compete with size goals.[13] Lifters on T Nation likewise log cardio, such as incline treadmill walks and bike sessions, alongside diet changes during cuts.[3]

Practitioners describe brisk walking, incline treadmill walking, stationary cycling, rowing and easy jogging as typical zone 2 formats, usually timed in sessions of roughly half an hour to an hour and paired with a calorie deficit for fat loss.[1][2][4] Aerobic training guidance cited on Wikipedia suggests at least 20 minutes, three times a week, for a training effect, and public-health bodies cite about 2.5 hours of moderate activity weekly.[2]
Lifters often add cardio after or on separate days from resistance training and some use heart-rate monitors or the conversation test to stay in the zone.[1][3]

Overuse injuries, overtraining syndrome, and relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) in athletes with high training volume and low intake are reported risks of aerobic training, and overuse injuries are reported as more common in athletes under 19.[2] For HIIT, the American College of Sports Medicine advises medical consultation for people with coronary heart disease, and the sources describe injury risk from fatigue and rapid blood-pressure spikes.[8]
Zone 2 has no universally accepted definition, so published numbers for intensity vary between sources.[1]

A randomized trial in overweight and obese adults compared 12 weeks of aerobic, resistance or combined exercise training and examined cardiovascular risk factors.[14] A 2023 dose-response meta-analysis linked more physical activity with lower cardiovascular disease, cancer and mortality.[2] A 2025 narrative review in Sports Medicine by Storoschuk and colleagues examined zone 2 training in relation to mitochondrial capacity and cardiorespiratory fitness in the general population.[9] A 2026 randomized crossover study in 10 trained men found peak fat oxidation rose after glycogen-depleting exercise, most when paired with a low-carbohydrate diet.[9] No studies found specifically on zone 2 for facial leanness.

lore.intro: In looksmaxxing forums, cardio is mostly framed as a leanmaxxing tool alongside diet, with debate about how it fits with lifting and whether it reduces face fat.[6][7]
